lesson.title: Selection Sort: Repeatedly Picking the Smallest
lesson.summary: Selection sort builds a sorted list by repeatedly scanning the unsorted portion for its minimum element and swapping that minimum into place at the front.
lesson.body:
Selection sort is one of the most direct ways to sort a list, and it builds naturally on two ideas you already know: traversing a list element by element, and comparing values with operators like less-than. The strategy is simple: repeatedly find the smallest remaining value and move it to where it belongs.

Concretely, selection sort splits the list into a sorted portion at the front (initially empty) and an unsorted portion at the back (initially the whole list). On each pass, it traverses the unsorted portion to find the index of the smallest element, then swaps that element into the first open position of the sorted portion. That grows the sorted portion by one element and shrinks the unsorted portion by one, and the process repeats until the unsorted portion is empty.

def selection_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        min_index = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if arr[j] < arr[min_index]:
                min_index = j
        arr[i], arr[min_index] = arr[min_index], arr[i]
    return arr

Trace this by hand on arr = [29, 10, 14, 37, 13].

i = 0: scan the whole list for the smallest value. 10 at index 1 is the smallest. Swap arr[0] and arr[1]: the list becomes [10, 29, 14, 37, 13].

i = 1: scan indices 1 through 4, which hold [29, 14, 37, 13]. The smallest is 13 at index 4. Swap arr[1] and arr[4]: the list becomes [10, 13, 14, 37, 29].

i = 2: scan indices 2 through 4, which hold [14, 37, 29]. The smallest, 14, is already at index 2, so the swap leaves the list unchanged: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29].

i = 3: scan indices 3 through 4, which hold [37, 29]. The smallest is 29 at index 4. Swap arr[3] and arr[4]: the list becomes [10, 13, 14, 29, 37].

At this point every element except the last is in its final position, and since it is the only element left, the list is fully sorted: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37].

Notice that the inner loop always scans every remaining element, no matter how the list started out. Even if the list were already sorted, selection sort would still compare each unsorted element against the current minimum before moving on. That makes selection sort's performance O(n squared) in every case: best, worst, and average, since the number of comparisons only depends on the length of the list, not on the order of its elements. One thing selection sort does do well is minimize the number of swaps: it performs at most one swap per pass, so at most n minus 1 swaps total, which can matter if swapping elements is an expensive operation compared to comparing them.
